Real estate portal leads: how to reply on WhatsApp before other agencies do

The person who asked about your listing asked about the same apartment at three other agencies. Whoever books the viewing first usually wins. Here is how to set up your team to be that agency.

LVBy Lucas Vaz·October 12, 2026·8 min read

Key takeaways

  • Portal leads often inquire about the same property across several listings. The first useful reply sets the benchmark.
  • The first message should name the property, answer the question and propose a next step.
  • Three qualifying questions are enough at first: buy or rent, timeline and how they'll pay.
  • Offer two viewing times instead of asking “when works for you?”.
  • A lead with no owner is a lost lead: decide who answers in every time slot, weekends included.

Sunday, 9 p.m. A couple is on the couch scrolling through two-bedroom apartments. They find one that looks perfect, close to their son's school, and send a message. But the same apartment appears in four listings, from four different agencies. They message all of them.

Monday at 8:15 a.m., one agency has already replied, confirmed the unit is available and offered a viewing Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. The other three will reply at some point during the day. The viewing is already booked.

That's how the race for real estate portal leads works. You rarely compete on price or on the property, which is often the same one. You compete on who shows up first with an answer that actually helps.

Why a portal lead is different from any other lead

Three things make this lead special, and they all point the same way: speed.

  • They're comparing the same property. When several agencies list the same apartment, the service is the only difference. The first useful reply becomes the benchmark.
  • Commitment is low. Tapping “I'm interested” takes a second. A buyer can inquire about ten homes in one evening and clearly remember two or three.
  • They show up after hours. People browse homes at night and on weekends, when they have time. That's exactly when the office is closed.

A study published in Harvard Business Review found that, for web leads, trying to make contact within the first hour sharply increases the odds of a meaningful conversation. We go through the numbers and the caveats in our piece on speed to lead. In real estate, with the same property listed several times, that logic gets even stronger.

Form or WhatsApp button: what changes in the first message

A lead can arrive in two ways, and that changes what you're allowed to send on the official WhatsApp API.

The customer tapped the listing's WhatsApp button. They sent the first message, so the conversation is already open. You have 24 hours to reply freely, with text, photos, a video tour, a location pin. Each new message from them resets the clock. If that rule is new to you, read about the WhatsApp 24-hour window.

The customer filled out a form and the portal sent you their number. Now you're the one starting the conversation. On the official API, that takes two things: a Meta-approved message template and the person's permission to be contacted by your business. Meta's opt-in policy requires that people clearly know they're agreeing to receive messages, and from which business. Check what the portal form tells the customer. If in doubt, a quick phone call works, and at the end you ask whether you can continue on WhatsApp.

A short template for that case, with no sales tone, that invites a reply:

Hi [name], this is [agent] from [agency]. We received your request for information about the apartment on [street], listing [code]. Can I send you photos and details here?

Once they reply, the window opens and you carry on as usual.

What to write in the first reply

The first reply has three jobs: show you know which property they mean, answer what they asked and propose a next step. No “Dear customer”, no link to your whole website.

For a purchase:

Hi Rachel! I'm Phil from Horizon Realty. The apartment on Maple Street (listing 4821) is available: 2 bedrooms, 730 sq ft, 1 parking spot, HOA fee of US$310 a month.

Are you planning to get a mortgage or pay cash? I ask because I can get you a rough payment estimate before the viewing.

For a rental:

Hi Daniel! This is Marina from Horizon. The house on Oak Avenue (listing 3307) is still available: US$1,900 a month, utilities not included. Small pets are allowed.

When do you need to move in?

If the property is already rented or sold, say so right away and offer similar options. This is where many agencies lose the customer, out of embarrassment over giving bad news:

Hi Rachel! That apartment sold last week, I'm sorry. I have two similar ones in the same neighborhood, in the same price range. Want me to send you the photos?

Qualifying questions that don't feel like an interrogation

The classic mistake is sending a full questionnaire in the second message: income, job, marital status, number of kids. The customer just wanted to know whether the apartment has a balcony.

At first, three questions are enough. The rest comes up naturally during the viewing.

QuestionWhy it mattersHow to ask
Buy or rent?Changes everythingThe listing often answers it
When?Separates urgent from curious“When do you need to move?”
How will they pay?Mortgage, cash, guarantor“Mortgage or cash?”
Want to visit?The goal of the chatOffer two time slots

One question per message, always tied to something you just said. “I can get you a payment estimate” justifies asking about a mortgage. Without that reason, the same question feels like screening.

How to book the viewing without endless back-and-forth

“When works for you?” triggers a chain of messages that takes days: the customer says “next week”, you ask which day, they say “Wednesday”, you ask what time, they disappear. Offer closed choices:

I can show you the apartment tomorrow at 6:30 p.m. or Saturday at 10 a.m. Which is better for you?

Once confirmed, put everything in one message so it's easy to find on the day:

Great, Rachel! Viewing on Saturday at 10 a.m.

Address: 210 Maple Street, unit 52. I'll be the one meeting you, Phil. If you need to change the time, just let me know here.

The day before, send a short reminder. If more than 24 hours have passed since the customer's last message, that reminder has to be an approved template. Since it's about an appointment the customer booked, it tends to fit the utility category, the cheaper one, as long as it carries no offer. In the end, Meta decides the category.

Who answers: assigning leads to agents

At many agencies, leads land in an email inbox or on a front-desk phone and wait for someone to “grab” them. That's where the hours that decide the viewing get lost.

A good distribution rule is simple enough to fit in one sentence. Some options:

  • By area: each agent covers certain neighborhoods. Works when the agent truly knows the area.
  • By type: one team for rentals, another for sales. Makes sense because questions and timelines are very different.
  • Round robin: the next lead goes to the next agent on the list. The fairest option and the easiest to explain.

Whatever the rule, add a deadline: if the agent hasn't replied within 10 minutes during business hours, the lead goes back to the queue and on to the next agent. It sounds harsh, but it protects the customer and, at the end of the month, the whole team's commissions. Speed for the customer comes before fairness among agents.

In a shared inbox like Kontaro's, everyone answers from the agency's single number, each conversation shows who owns it, and the history stays with the business, not on the phone of someone who left. When a lead moves to another agent, always leave a one-line summary: “wants a high floor, has a dog, pre-approved up to US$400k”.

Weekend coverage and the lead who went quiet

Run a quick calculation with hypothetical numbers. An agency gets 150 portal leads a month. If a third arrive between Saturday afternoon and Sunday, that's 50 leads a month waiting until Monday. In a market where people inquire about the same property across several listings, many of them will tour with whoever replied on Sunday.

Three ways to cover the weekend, which can be combined:

  1. A rotating on-call agent. One agent per weekend replies to new leads, even if only to book a viewing for Monday.
  2. An AI that knows your listings. Trained on your listings, it confirms availability, shares prices, asks the qualifying questions and proposes viewing times. When the conversation needs an agent, it hands it over with a summary.
  3. A Monday 8 a.m. list. Anyone who came in over the weekend and hasn't been answered is the first task of the week, before coffee.

In Kontaro, the AI learns from the agency's website and from listing spreadsheets, and you can let it reply on its own or just prepare drafts for the on-call agent to approve.

And the customer who got the photos and went silent? Not a lost cause. Most of the time they're still touring other homes. A message two or three days later with something new (a similar listing that just came in, an answer about the HOA) often reopens the conversation. We have ready-made templates in follow-up messages that don't sound pushy.

Start next Monday

On Monday, before anything else, pull the portal leads that came in over the past weekend and write down when each one got its first reply. If the typical answer is “Monday morning”, you already know where to start.

Pick an agent for the next weekend shift, save the three first-message templates from this piece with real details from your listings, and agree on the 10-minute rule with the team. You don't need a long meeting. You need one sentence written on the wall and someone who checks that it's being followed.

Frequently asked questions

How fast should a real estate agency respond to a portal lead?

Within minutes, ideally. Buyers and renters often inquire about the same property across several listings at once, and whoever replies first with useful information tends to lead the conversation and book the viewing.

Can I message a portal lead who filled out a form on WhatsApp?

On the official API, you need the person's opt-in to hear from your business, and the first message must be an approved template. Check what the portal form tells the customer. If they tapped the listing's WhatsApp button, the conversation is already open.

What questions should I ask to qualify a real estate lead?

Start with three: are they buying or renting, when do they need to move, and how do they plan to pay (mortgage, cash, or for rentals, deposit and guarantor). The rest can wait for the viewing.

How do I distribute leads fairly among agents?

Pick one simple rule (area, property type or round robin), set a deadline for the agent to reply and send the lead back to the queue if it's missed. Speed for the customer comes before fairness among agents.
